rules.title: obsidian-tdd artifact present and tracked
rules.source: v3 PLAN §11 D6–D10 — the plugin boundary; the obsidian-tdd plugin's tdd.json is the test-discipline evidence a repo commits
rules.lesson: A plugin is known by its artifact, not by its data: baseline asks whether tdd.json is there and whether git tracks it, and never opens it — the file's schema, its covers[] and its source commit are obsidian-tdd's own business (D7).
rules.rationale: Membership is the gate, and membership is a fact about the config, not a guess about the tree (v4): a plugin whose NAME is a key of baseline.config.json `plugins` is a MEMBER of this repo's trust circle, and this rule is a BLOCKER for it — the artifact must be present and git must say what the config expects, or the build fails. A plugin the config never named is a SUGGESTION: baseline offers it in the report, resolves this rule n/a, excludes it from the exit gate, and it can never fail a build. So absent-and-not-a-member is n/a; member-and-missing is a blocker (D8, as amended by the v4 membership model — one always-on rule per plugin, gated by adoption rather than by presence). When a member's artifact is there the one further question is git's (D9): tdd.json is committed evidence, so the default expects it tracked, and a config-vs-git disagreement is the finding. Every finding leaves .baseline/log/PLUG-01.log recording the path inspected, the config values used, the membership fact and git's answer (D10).
rules.fix: If this repo has adopted obsidian-tdd, install the plugin and run it once so tdd.json lands at the repo root (the install command in the finding is a placeholder for the plugin's own instructions), then commit tdd.json. If it has not, `baseline trust remove obsidian-tdd` deletes the key and this rule goes back to n/a — nothing here fails a repo that never chose the tool. Adoption and location are the same declaration: {"plugins": {"obsidian-tdd": {}}} adopts at the defaults, {"plugins": {"obsidian-tdd": {"path": "tools/tdd.json", "ignored": false}}} adopts with an override, and `baseline trust add obsidian-tdd` writes either for you.

rules.title: graphify graph present and gitignored
rules.source: v3 PLAN §11 D6–D10 — the plugin boundary; graphify's graphify-out/ is a derived knowledge graph, rebuilt from the tree
rules.lesson: The graph is a plugin artifact: the only questions baseline asks are whether graphify-out/ is there, how old it is, and whether git ignores it. `Built from commit:` is a line in a file graphify owns, and reading it would make the verdict depend on the plugin's format (D7).
rules.rationale: Membership is the gate, and membership is a fact about the config, not a guess about the tree (v4): a plugin whose NAME is a key of baseline.config.json `plugins` is a MEMBER of this repo's trust circle, and this rule is a BLOCKER for it — an absent graph is named once, with the install command, and it fails the build. A repo that never adopted graphify gets a SUGGESTION instead: this rule resolves n/a, stays out of the exit gate, and cannot fail anything. So absent-and-not-a-member is n/a; member-and-missing is a blocker (D8, as amended by the v4 membership model). When a member's graph is present the one further question is git's (D9): a derived store belongs in .gitignore, so the default expects it ignored, and a tracked graphify-out/ is the finding (config says ignored, git says tracked). Every finding leaves .baseline/log/PLUG-02.log recording the path inspected, the config values used, the membership fact and git's answer (D10).
rules.fix: If this repo has adopted graphify, install the plugin and build the graph so graphify-out/ exists (the install command in the finding is a placeholder for the plugin's own instructions), and add graphify-out/ to .gitignore — the pass is deterministic (an AST read of the tree, no LLM), so the same commit always rebuilds the same graph, and `baseline trust stamp` commits the hashes CI reads. If it has not, `baseline trust remove graphify` deletes the key and this rule goes back to n/a. Adoption and location are the same declaration: {"plugins": {"graphify": {}}} adopts at the defaults, {"plugins": {"graphify": {"path": "graphify-out", "ignored": true}}} adopts with an override, and `baseline trust add graphify` writes either for you.

rules.title: okf-rag bundle present
rules.source: v3 PLAN §11 D6–D10 — the plugin boundary; okf-rag's bundle is the concept store `baseline explain` addresses by concept id, at $BASELINE_OKF_BUNDLE
rules.lesson: The bundle is addressed by path or env and never read during check: no verdict depends on a retrieval (§1 V3), and the audit `explain --audit` resolves by filename alone. Presence, kind, age and git state are the whole question (D7).
rules.rationale: Membership is the gate, and membership is a fact about the config, not a guess about the environment (v4): a plugin whose NAME is a key of baseline.config.json `plugins` is a MEMBER of this repo's trust circle, and this rule is a BLOCKER for it — an unset or missing bundle is named once, with the install command, and it fails the build. $BASELINE_OKF_BUNDLE sets a member's path but never creates membership: CI clones tracked files, not a shell, so an env-created member would gate differently on two machines. A repo that never named okf-rag gets a SUGGESTION: this rule resolves n/a and stays out of the exit gate. So absent-and-not-a-member is n/a; member-and-missing is a blocker (D8, as amended by the v4 membership model). The bundle usually lives outside the repo, and a path outside the repo is not asked the gitignore question at all (D9); a bundle kept inside is a derived store, so the default expects it ignored. Every finding leaves .baseline/log/PLUG-03.log recording the path inspected, the config values used, the membership fact and git's answer (D10).
rules.fix: If this repo has adopted okf-rag, install the plugin (the install command in the finding is a placeholder for the plugin's own instructions) and point baseline at the bundle: export BASELINE_OKF_BUNDLE=<dir>, or declare the path in the same entry that declares membership. If it has not, `baseline trust remove okf-rag` deletes the key and this rule goes back to n/a. Adoption is the key itself: {"plugins": {"okf-rag": {}}} adopts at the defaults (path from the env var), {"plugins": {"okf-rag": {"path": "/abs/path/to/bundle", "ignored": true}}} adopts with an override, and `baseline trust add okf-rag` writes either for you. `baseline gen okf-concepts` stages the per-rule concepts the bundle is built from.
